picked.body: 기사 이해를 돕기위해 AI를 활용해 제작한 이미지입니다. 베트남의 암호화폐 시장 규모가 동남아에서 두 번째로 큰 것으로 나타났다. 블록체인 분석업체 체이널리시스(Chainalysis)의 최신 데이터에 따르면, 2025년 7월부터 지난 6월까지 1년간 베트남 내 암호화폐 거래 규모는 1,222억 달러로 싱가포르(2,841억 달러)에 이어 동남아 2위를 기록했다. 보고서는 암호화폐 경제에 초점을 맞춰, 2025년 7월부터 지난 6월까지 △중앙화·탈중앙화 거래소 △개인 간(P2P) 거래 △국경 간 자금 흐름 △기관 대상 플랫폼 등 여러 경로로 비트코인·이더리움·스테이블코인 및 기타 토큰이 블록체인을 따라 이동한 흐름과 활동을 추적했다. 분석 결과에 따르면, 베트남 암호화폐 시장은 역내 다른 금융 중심지와 차별화된 양상을 보였다. 베트남과 태국, 필리핀은 P2P 활동이 두드러진 반면, 싱가포르와 호주는 금융기관 대상 플랫폼을 통한 거래가 눈에 띄게 늘었다. P2P 거래는 구매자와 판매자를 이어주는 플랫폼을 통해 개인 간에 자산을 직접 이전하는 방식이다. 이러한 방식은 암호화폐 매매·송금·결제 등에 쓰일 수 있지만, 거래 데이터만으로는 개별 이체의 구체적인 목적을 파악할 수 없다. 같은 기간 베트남·필리핀·태국에서는 1만 달러 미만 소액 P2P 이체가 모두 540만 건 기록됐다. 전 세계 암호화폐 시장에서 3개국이 차지하는 비중은 거래액 기준 2.5%에 불과하나 소액 P2P 이체 건수는 무려 14.4%를 차지했다. 자세히 살펴보면, 이들 3개국의 국내 이체 건수의 80% 이상은 1,000달러 미만이었는데, 평균 이체액은 618달러로 세계 평균(1,210달러)을 크게 밑돌았다. 스테이블코인은 베트남 디지털 자산 시장의 중요 요소로서 그 비중을 확대하고 있다. 스테이블코인은 주로 미국 달러화 대비 안정적 가치를 유지하도록 설계된 암호화폐의 일종으로, 지난 1년간 베트남 내 거래 규모는 69억 달러를 기록했다.

picked.t: Vietnam waives visas for Chinese tour groups to Nha Trang
picked.body: The visa-exemption policy took effect from Oct. 12 as part of the Vietnam-China Tourism Cooperation Year 2026–2027 and will remain in place until Dec. 31, 2027. The exemption applies to Chinese citizens holding valid ordinary passports who join all-inclusive tour packages organized by Vietnamese international travel agencies. Groups must consist of at least two travelers, and tours cannot exceed 30 days. They are only allowed to travel within Khanh Hoa. Under the scheme, eligible visitors must fly directly from mainland China to Cam Ranh International Airport, about 40 kilometers from downtown Nha Trang, and exit Vietnam through the same airport. The exemption does not apply to independent travelers, tourists without an eligible all-inclusive tour package, or those entering or departing Vietnam through other border checkpoints. Holders of passports issued by China's Hong Kong and Macau special administrative regions are excluded from the policy. Vietnam's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Ministry of Public Security have been assigned to issue guidance on implementation procedures and entry requirements. Khanh Hoa used to be a favorite destination for Chinese tourists before Covid. In 2019, the province welcomed more than 2.5 million Chinese visitors, accounting for 75% of international visitors. According to the Khanh Hoa's Department of Culture, Sports and Tourism, the province received about 378,600 Chinese visitors in the first seven months this year, down more than 5.3%, making them the third largest foreign tourist source, behind South Korea and Russia. Nationwide, China remained Vietnam's largest source market for inbound tourism in the first nine months of the year, with 3.95 million arrivals, up 1.5% year-on-year.

picked.t: Ho Chi Minh City to eliminate 28 traffic bottlenecks by 2030
picked.body: Department director Tran Quang Lam outlined the goal during the "Citizens Ask – Government Answers" program on Oct. 11. He emphasized that resolving these hotspots remains a top municipal priority through 2030. Priority will be given to completing ongoing and planned projects to ease congestion at key locations. These include the My Thuy and An Phu interchanges, National Highway 13, the Nguyen Khoai bridge-and-road project, and Binh Tien. Lam noted that addressing the 28 bottlenecks is just one component of a broader infrastructure strategy. The city also aims to complete its wider transport network, improve regional connectivity, and develop new economic corridors. Surveys conducted prior to the city's administrative merger with Binh Duong and Ba Ria-Vung Tau provinces last year identified several persistent bottlenecks. These included the Hang Xanh intersection, Nguyen Tat Thanh Street, and the An Phu and My Thuy interchanges. Similar congestion issues plague intersections and industrial parks in the former Binh Duong and Ba Ria-Vung Tau areas. Beyond existing projects, authorities are studying plans to construct steel overpasses at various locations to further alleviate traffic. Transport hub Ho Chi Minh City serves as a major national and regional transportation hub, integrating aviation, maritime shipping, inland waterways, and railway networks. The megacity currently handles approximately 37% of Vietnam's air passenger traffic and 65% of its container cargo volume. However, widespread infrastructure bottlenecks and poorly integrated transport networks remain significant challenges. Localized congestion continues to hamper residents' daily lives, economic development, and the overall investment climate. Following the recent administrative merger, the city identified three primary focus areas for transport development. The immediate priority is eliminating existing bottlenecks. The second goal is completing backbone infrastructure and strengthening regional connectivity via ring roads, expressways, and national highways. The third priority involves expanding the metro network in alignment with the Transit-Oriented Development model. The city expects to largely complete its backbone transport infrastructure by 2030. However, the department warned that these initiatives alone will not sustain a megacity of 14 million residents, which is projected to reach 25 million in the future. Officials have identified the expansion of the urban railway network as the fundamental long-term solution. The metro network is expected to expand to 255 km by 2030, and to roughly 500 km over the subsequent decade. Under the revised master plan, the network will ultimately reach 1,500 km in total length. "These are not merely targets the city has set; preparations have already been made to ensure that implementation is feasible," Lam said. He noted that metro projects now benefit from special administrative mechanisms that grant the city greater autonomy. New urban development policies are also helping authorities mobilize resources, diversify investments, and accelerate implementation. Department of Finance deputy director Truong Tan Vu confirmed that transportation infrastructure remains a top investment priority. Projects are being categorized to ensure the efficient use of resources. Funding will focus on initiatives that address congestion, mitigate flooding, and boost economic development. The city has allocated approximately VND500 trillion (US$19.29 billion) for investment programs during the 2026-2030 period. This includes VND200 trillion earmarked for 98 transport projects, which covers the initiatives targeting the 28 congestion hotspots. Another VND120 trillion is allocated for 37 regional connectivity projects. An additional VND50 trillion is designated for 59 projects addressing severe flooding. The city will also continue relocating homes situated along canals and waterways. These efforts will be combined with urban renovation and transport infrastructure improvements to enhance the overall living environment.

picked.t: Earning more, feeling less: the quiet burnout of young Vietnamese workers
picked.body: The 27-year-old software engineer from southern Tay Ninh Province glanced at the screen, turned his phone face down and immediately went back to coding. Minh earns VND60-70 million a month from three jobs. He works full time at a tech company, freelances remotely for overseas clients at night and handles system maintenance for a startup on weekends. His income puts Minh in a much higher bracket than his peers, but he cannot remember the last time money made him smile. Minh's world is confined to the space between his two screens. Both lunch and dinner take place at his desk, with a Styrofoam takeout box sitting right beside his keyboard. The strong cup of coffee he drinks every morning now serves only one purpose: fighting off sleepiness. The soccer shoes placed in the corner of his rented room haven't been worn in over a year, and the acoustic guitar propped up next to his wardrobe has two snapped strings. Every time he lies down to watch a movie for more than 15 minutes, he turns on his computer to check on project progress. "The digits in my account keep going up, while I just stay numb. If I take even a single day off, I feel like I'm making a mistake," he says. Phuong, 28, a teacher in HCMC, has a similar schedule. After finishing her daytime classes at a public school, she teaches evening classes at a foreign language center, translates study abroad applications, and tutors students on both days of the weekend. Her income of nearly VND50 million per month allows Phuong to buy her own vehicle, send money home to her parents every month, and become the "perfect" role model in her family's eyes. In the classroom, she maintains a neat, energetic appearance, but once she leaves, she falls into a state of exhaustion. Her dry, raspy throat makes her dread everyday conversations. Messages from relatives often sit in her unread inbox for days. On her 28th birthday, she returned to her rented room at 10 p.m. with two bouquets of flowers and a handwritten card from a student, placed them all on the floor, and sat leaning against the wall until nearly 1 a.m. "Students congratulate me, and friends praise how capable I am. What I fear most is that I no longer know how to feel happy," Phuong states. Vuong Nguyen Toan Thien, medical director at Lumos Psychological Counseling and Therapy Center, says Minh and Phương are classic examples of high-functioning anhedonia, or the state of performing well at work despite emotional burnout. There are no official statistics on the number of people experiencing this condition in Vietnam or globally. But Thien says patients like Minh and Phuong are appearing more and more frequently in counseling rooms. The dangerous thing about this condition is that patients still excel at making money, communicate skillfully, and maintain a facade of success, but have lost the reflex to feel joy. They do not collapse from a major crisis, but burn out gradually due to the non-stop, frantic grind. This phenomenon stems from prolonged work structures, pressure to advance in one’s career, and the self-imposed psychological urge not to fall behind. The modern workplace encourages this through the trap of "moralizing busyness", where replying to emails at midnight is praised as dedication, sleeping four hours a night is seen as responsible, and working through weekends is glorified. But some companies claim this pressure does not entirely come from one-sided demands by management, but also partly from employees pushing themselves into overload. Nguyen Thu Trang, HR director of a software development company in HCMC, says tech companies have now shifted almost entirely to performance-based evaluations (OKRs/KPIs) instead of attendance, but unspoken competition between young employees often drives up the workload. "Many people voluntarily take on extra work, submit reports at midnight, or work through the weekend out of fear of falling behind or to prove their competence for rapid promotion. The company has a policy of turning off internal notifications after 7 p.m. and encourages taking time off, but quite a few employees still secretly open their computers to keep working," Trang says. Employees' silent burnout is actually a major risk for businesses, because after a phase of "peak productivity," they often abruptly quit or experience a severe drop in performance, causing the company to spend money on recruitment and retraining someone else from scratch, she explains. According to estimates by the World Health Organization and the International Labour Organization, working 55 hours or more per week increases the risk of ischemic heart disease by about 17% and stroke by 35% compared to working 35-40 hours. In 2016 alone, some 745,000 deaths globally were linked to working overtime. picked.t: Hanoi adds greenery to transport infrastructure to reduce urban heat
picked.body: The Hanoi Department of Construction has directed local agencies to design and pilot greening projects across key transport infrastructure. The initiative will target three urban railway pillars along Nguyen Trai Street, the Le Van Luong-To Huu underpass, the Le Van Luong-Lang Ha overpass, and various downtown bus shelters. Greenery has already been successfully integrated into several of the city's existing transport facilities. Along Thang Long Boulevard, thousands of date palms currently line both sides of the underpasses and the central median. These palms serve as the primary canopy for the area, sheltering a diverse layer of smaller plant species cultivated beneath them. The 600-meter Trung Hoa underpass, featuring three traffic lanes across each of its 12-meter-wide sides, is now lined with climbing plants cascading down its concrete walls. Above the facility, various trees and flowers are planted in tiered layers, including Wrightia religiosa, crinum lilies, Arabian jasmine, hibiscus, canna lilies, and crepe myrtles. The route is primarily planted with Vernonia elliptica, a fast-growing climber known for its soft, naturally cascading branches. As the plants mature, they create lush green curtains that provide shade, filter dust, and cool the surrounding environment. The cascading foliage can extend 4–5 m downward. Watering schedules are adjusted according to weather conditions and the season. In summer and autumn, plants are typically watered at night or in the early morning. Clusters of slender-stemmed bamboo currently line the base of the overpass at the Le Van Luong-Lang Ha intersection. Authorities are now planning a pilot project to cover the bridge's supporting walls with climbing plants. The greenery will span approximately 200 sq.m, strategically divided into sections to complement the structure's existing architecture. At the intersection of National Highways 5 and 1, rows of small-leaved tropical almond trees—also known as Taiwan almonds—line the median and both sides of the approach roads. Spaced approximately three meters apart, the trees form a continuous green corridor. Vehicles traveling from National Highway 5 toward Bac Ninh pass beneath the shade of trees along the route as they approach Hanoi's eastern gateway. On the afternoon of Oct. 9, workers planted several species, including Monstera deliciosa, silver pothos, spider plants, and lantana, in pots attached to steel frames around the pillars of the Cat Linh-Ha Dong urban railway. Under the plan, the plants will climb the frames to cover the pillars in greenery without attaching directly to the concrete. This approach is designed to improve the urban landscape and reduce concrete surface temperatures. A section of Ring Road 2 has also been covered with densely planted layers of greenery along both sides. An automatic irrigation system maintains moisture levels and supports plant growth. At the Vo Chi Cong-Hoang Quoc Viet-Hoang Hoa Tham intersection, various plants grow beneath the overpass, around the roundabout, and along the ramps leading to the elevated roadway. picked.t: HCMC flood-control project turns roadside homes into ‘basements’
picked.body: Over the past three months, contractors have elevated the road to tackle chronic flooding caused by high tides, leaving the ground floors of many properties far beneath the newly raised surface. The VND93 billion (US$3.58 million) project, managed by the former Binh Thanh District construction authority, covers 1.2 kilometers and includes a new drainage system that is still being built. Residents whose homes now sit up to 1.5 meters below the road rely on improvised steps made from plastic chairs, buckets, sandbags and other materials to get in and out. Residents whose homes now sit up to 1.5 meters below the road rely on improvised steps made from plastic chairs, buckets, sandbags and other materials to get in and out. Residents whose homes now sit up to 1.5 meters below the road rely on improvised steps made from plastic chairs, buckets, sandbags and other materials to get in and out. Doan Van Thuan, 38, climbs over a 1.2-meter-high stack of sandbags outside his home, which he spent the past two months building to reach the street. His doorway once stood nearly half a meter above the road, but his living room now resembles a sunken basement. The steep drop from the road into Thuan’s house makes it difficult to move a motorbike indoors, forcing him to control the vehicle carefully to keep it from sliding downhill. “If I raise the floor, the ceiling will become too low,” Thuan says. “Rebuilding the entire house is the only real solution, but I simply cannot afford it.” A nearby supermarket also sits far below street level, with customers using makeshift wooden stairs, compacted soil and flattened cardboard to enter. Deliveries become difficult as workers have to move goods across loose gravel, construction debris and uneven ground. At Truong Xuan Thang’s coffee shop, customer numbers have dropped by more than half since the road was raised above the level of his storefront. “As a tenant, I cannot rebuild a property that does not belong to me,” he says. “The longer the construction continues, the fewer customers we have.” Many homes along the road appear dark and damp as heavy rain and tidal flooding repeatedly send moisture indoors. Several businesses have closed and put up signs offering their premises for lease after losing customers during the prolonged construction. Several businesses have closed and put up signs offering their premises for lease after losing customers during the prolonged construction. Some families say they have spent nearly VND10 million building temporary concrete steps just to maintain access to their homes while the roadwork continues. Outside Van Hau’s eatery, construction creates clouds of dust in dry weather and thick mud after rain, forcing staff to wash the area every day. Customers stay away as pools of muddy water block the entrance and leave little room for motorbike parking. “When it rains heavily, water rushes inside until the whole place looks like a pond,” Hau says. “It can take a full day to drain, and our furniture gets damaged.” Local authorities say Dang Thuy Tram Street lies in a naturally low-lying area affected by tidal surges from the Vam Thuat River and Xuyen Tam Canal, making the road elevation and drainage upgrade necessary. Because the main stormwater drainage lines are still being completed, drainage capacity along the street remains limited. The project is about 70% complete. Contractors are preparing to lay the final asphalt surface and finish sidewalks and other streetscape works, with the upgraded road expected to open by the end of 2026. picked.t: Vietnam carriers gear up for tourism boom with new Asia, Europe services
picked.body: Vietnam's newest carrier Sun PhuQuoc Airways plans to launch its first international route between Phu Quoc and Moscow on Nov. 13 with an Airbus A330 aircraft as Russia is now one of Vietnam's fastest-growing tourism markets. Before that, on Oct. 15, it will launch a new service between Ho Chi Minh City and China's Shanghai megacity. Vietjet Air has also announced plans to expand its international network with flights linking Ho Chi Minh City with Male, the capital of the Maldives, with passengers transiting in Colombo. The service is scheduled to begin on Dec. 5. It will also launch new services between Hanoi and Prague, Czechia, and Almaty, Kazakhstan, this month. Vietravel Airlines said it will start flying between Hanoi and Shenzhen, known as the Silicon Valley of China, on Nov. 26. The expansion into Asia and Europe come as Vietnam received 17.7 million international visitors in the first nine months of 2026, up 14.5% year-on-year, bucking a declining trend seen in several Southeast Asian destinations like Singapore, Cambodia, and Thailand. Mainland China was Vietnam's largest inbound market, with 3.95 million visitors or 22.3% of all arrivals. Russia was third with 1.1 million visitors, up over 160% year-on-year. The number of Russian visitors is forecast to reach a record 1.5 million this year. European arrivals increased by more than 50%, while arrivals from markets like the United States, Australia, and India also recorded strong growth. This has helped Vietnam shrug off its earlier dependence on just one or two major Asian inbound markets. Industry insiders have urged the government to extend visa exemptions to nationals of major markets such as China and India and boost air connectivity with global tourism hubs to help the country reach its target of 25 million international visitors this year.

picked.t: US hikes pepper imports from Vietnam, slashes purchases from elsewhere
picked.body: Vietnam’s shipments amounted to 44,100 tons during the period, with value rising by 21% to US$331 million, according to the United States International Trade Commission. In volume terms, Vietnam accounted for 80.4% of the U.S. imports of 54,900 tons, up from 69% a year ago. Overall, the U.S. imported pepper worth $407 million in the seven months, up 5.4%. Imports from two other major suppliers, Indonesia and India, declined by 59.3% and 17.2% in volume. Shipments from Brazil and China rose 6.8% and 4.8%, but they accounted for only 4% and 0.9% of the supply. Vietnam’s Agency for Foreign Trade said pepper exports to the U.S. rose thanks to steady supply, improved quality, and lower prices. The average price of Vietnamese pepper fell marginally to $7,499 per ton while that of Indonesian exports went up 18% to $8,691. Vietnam also offers a wide range of pepper products for different market segments, including whole black peppercorns catering to food manufacturers, ground pepper, white pepper, and packaged products for the restaurant and retail sectors, the agency added. The Vietnam Pepper and Spice Association expected shipments to the U.S. to continue to rise in the remaining months of the year. But businesses need to explore new processing methods to add value to their products while ensuring food safety, traceability, and quality, it added.

picked.t: More police, fewer snatchers: Tourists say Vietnam feels safer
picked.body: Luke's first visit to Ho Chi Minh City last April began with an unwelcome encounter outside Saigon Square, one of the city's popular shopping hubs. But what happened after he was targeted by a group of shoeshiners left a lasting impression — and made him eager to return. Luke was waiting for his girlfriend and looking at his phone when a group of shoeshiners approached and immediately took off his shoes. "Even though I declined they were very pushy, and intent on providing the service without me asking for it or approving it." Instead of confirming a price, the men chatted about England, football, and other subjects they might expect to interest a tourist. When they eventually left, Luke discovered that his wallet had been emptied of more money than he had agreed to pay. "They stole money from my wallet," he says. The incident shocked him, but it did not sour his view of Ho Chi Minh City or Vietnam. "I have been looking up travel around Southeast Asia and I'm aware that tourist traps happen and I'm not particularly sad that I fell for one," he says. "It just made me more vigilant in the future." What happened next helped turn an unpleasant encounter into a more reassuring story about the city. On April 10, HCMC police caught a group of shoeshiners red-handed while they were extorting money from tourists. Officers said they had kept tabs on them for some time and knew the groups targeted newcomers in central areas. Luke was impressed by the response, saying he was "overwhelmed and surprised by how efficiently everything is handled." He said he was used to investigations in English cities being hampered by red tape and regulations. "So to see HCMC police act so quickly and efficiently in a way that put the people first was really amazing." Luke's experience reflects a broader sentiment among foreign tourists who say they feel increasingly comfortable exploring Vietnam, even as they remain alert to scams. Australian Carl Tomich first visited Vietnam in 2016, when warnings about street theft targeting foreigners made him cautious about his belongings. He kept them close, and never had anything stolen. When he returned in 2024 and began exploring the country for a longer period, those concerns had largely faded, he says. "I felt much more relaxed. Street theft barely crossed my mind." He has spent more than a year in Vietnam in total and said he never had anything stolen. "I felt safer and less concerned when I returned." Alex Reeves, a visitor from the U.K., also recalls hearing warnings about bag snatching when he first arrived in Vietnam. "These days I don't hear people mention it much." He credits the government's efforts to deter crime for the change in perception. Police patrols and helpful locals For some visitors, the sense of security comes not from a dramatic police intervention but from ordinary experiences on the streets. Joshua, a British tourist on his third visit to Vietnam, is spending 21 days in Ho Chi Minh City and says personal safety had not been a major concern. "I haven't really worried about anything while in Vietnam. People are in general very helpful and friendly." The presence of police officers in the downtown area at night also helped put him at ease. He says it has made him feel "very secure" and less concerned about being robbed or attacked by strangers. Reeves has noticed a similar police presence in central Hanoi. "When I am in downtown areas such as Hoan Kiem, I am aware of an increase in police at certain times." Vietnam was ranked among the world's 10 safest destinations for tourists, alongside Singapore, in the safety and security category of the World Economic Forum's 2026 Travel and Tourism Development Index. Authorities report declines in several categories of crimes in the country's two largest cities. In Ho Chi Minh City, street crime, organized crime, professional criminal activity, and repeat offending have fallen sharply, Deputy Minister of Public Security Le Quoc Hung said at a conference on Sept. 28. The decline has left the city's once-renowned robber hunting police unit with little work to do, he said. "People who have to hit the streets early in the morning or late at night are no longer worried as they used to be." In Hanoi, crimes against social order fell by 12.09% in the first nine months of 2026, according to data reported at the Central Public Security Party Committee conference on Sept. 30. Tomich says he felt particularly safe in Hanoi compared with places where he had previously lived. "Vietnam is one of the places where I've felt safest." He speaks about regularly seeing fights and seeing news reports about knife attacks and gang crime in his hometown. "I've also been targeted at random several times, including being held up at knifepoint and having my phone stolen. I've never experienced anything like that in Vietnam." picked.t: 베트남 하노이시, 아파트 분양시장 ‘꽁꽁’…3분기 흡수율 31% 불과
picked.body: 기사 이해를 돕기위해 AI를 활용해 제작한 이미지입니다. 베트남 수도 하노이의 아파트 분양 시장이 꽁꽁 얼어붙은 것으로 나타났다. 글로벌 부동산 컨설팅 업체 애비슨영(Avison Young)이 최근 내놓은 3분기 시장 보고서에 따르면, 하반기 들어 하노이 아파트 분양가 상승세가 크게 둔화된 것으로 확인됐다. 앞서 2015년 말부터 상반기까지 이어졌던 분양가 급등세는 3분기 1.5~2.3% 상승에 그쳤다. 보고서에 따르면, 현재 하노이 신규 아파트 평균 분양가는 ㎡당 4,180달러로 잠정 집계됐다. 지역별 평균 분양가는 동부와 서부 외곽 도시 지역의 고급 아파트가 ㎡당 3,300~4,500달러 사이에 형성돼 있으며, 도심과 서호(Tay Ho) 지역은 ㎡당 5,500~9,800달러로 이보다 높은 수준을 보이고 있다. 애비슨영은 “아파트 분양가가 실수요자 대부분의 지불 능력을 넘어서면서, 3분기 흡수율은 31%에 그쳤다”고 설명했다. 앞서 지난해 3분기 흡수율은 70~80%를 기록한 바 있다. 또다른 부동산 컨설팅 업체 나이트프랭크(Knight Frank) 또한 3분기 흡수율이 38%로 급락했다는 보고서를 내놨다. 이는 신규 공급분과 재고를 합친 것으로, 2024년 이후 최저치에 해당한다. 전체 판매량 또한 전분기 대비 40%, 전년 동기 대비 52% 감소했는데, 동사는 “아파트 사용 기한에 대한 우려가 커지면서 수요는 실거주 목적 매수자 쪽으로 옮겨갔다”고 풀이했다. 업계에 따르면, 올 들어 높은 금리와 늘어나는 신규 공급은 아파트 분양 거래가 감소하는 주요 요인으로 작용하고 있다. 애비슨영에 따르면, 3분기 신규 공급된 아파트는 3,200여 세대로, 현재 분양 중인 물량은 1만1,500호까지 증가했다. 분양 흡수율이 크게 감소한 가운데 고급 부문으로 편중된 수급 불균형은 좀처럼 완화될 기미를 보이지 않고 있다. 애비슨영에 따르면, 전체 신규 공급 물량의 80% 이상은 고급·하이엔드 아파트로 구성돼 있으며, 실수요가 높은 중저가 아파트 공급은 사실상 자취를 감춘 상태다. 실거주 목적의 수요자 역시 주택담보대출금리의 변동금리가 연 12~15%까지 오른 상황에서 매수를 꺼리는 모양새다. 분양 시장이 얼어붙은 가운데 매매 시장은 매수자 우위 시장으로 재편되고 있다. 애비슨영 관계자는 “상당수 매도자가 금융 부담에 직면한 가운데, 매수자들은 원금 상환 유예 기간이 끝난 집주인들에게 8~12%까지 가격 인하를 요구하고 있다”며 “포모(FOMO)로 인해 서둘러 매수에 나서던 구매자들은 이제 자산의 실질적인 가치를 평가하는 신중한 모습을 보이고 있다”고 전했다. 나이트프랭크에 따르면, 내년 말까지 하노이 분양 시장에는 약 3만5,000호의 아파트가 추가로 공급될 것으로 예상된다. 이 중 3분의 1 이상은 서부 지역에 집중될 전망이다. 현지 부동산 전문가들은 “막대한 분양이 예정돼 있어 경쟁이 심해지는 만큼, 개발사들은 가격 전략과 상품 구성, 금융 지원 정책을 신중하게 고민해야 한다”고 말했다.
